I was so excited that they had finally made a reusable cup for my Keurig model. I was looking forward to not having to pay for expensive K-cups, and also using a product that is more environmentally friendly. It's a little shocking at first to see what a flimsy product you get for the money. But I gave it a try. Unfortunately, I have yet to make a satisfactory cup of coffee with it. The main problems are that the coffee is weak, and fine grounds accumulate on the bottom of the cup. I have experimented with different coffees and grinds, but still haven't had a really good cup yet. I started the process to return it, but the return shipping was almost half of the cost! (I'm very disappointed with you too, Amazon!) So I decided to keep it for emergencies, but I doubt it will get much use. Waste of money.

So far, my only issue has been that it definitely is messier than using the normal pods.  A few times, the hinge has come loose when I am pulling it out of my machine and then coffee grounds go everywhere.  I am willing to deal with this nuisance seeing how I can enjoy my favorite flavored coffee and I hope in the future, I will be better at making sure the hinge is closed completely so I won't have a mess when I pull it out of the machine.

The official one from Keurig is better although both leave grounds in your cup. You also need more coffee as water pours through the mesh type filters faster and/or unevenly especially if your coffee is not perfectly ground. Before tossing your next K kup, open and inspect the grounds; you will not get that with a typical home grinder. A compromise is to buy lids and reuse the K-Cup plastic pods. You can do this, but we find shopping sales, especially at places like Costco, brings the price per cup down to where the convenience factor of just using the K-Cup type pods is 'almost' reasonable. Reusing a K-Cup pod brings cost per cup down closer to cost of regular brewed coffee at home. Taste wise? Again the grind matters making the use of the K-Kup (or equivalent) pods hard to beat.

The only problem is the carafe's glass is too thin, and the integrated filter holder makes it difficult to wash in smaller sinks. While rinsing it out I accidentally tapped it against the side of the sink, cracked it. I have a Hario and a Kalita carafe that I've had longer. They're made of thicker glass, and not having the integrated filter holder makes it much easier to wash them out safely.

It might work well for you if you use it at home under ideal circumstances, but for an at work setup, it didn't work out for me.

I have mixed feelings about the metal filter. It makes perfectly good Aeropress coffee, so I didn't feel like I was missing out on flavor. The issue was in the usage flow. With a paper filter, once I have made the coffee I just eject the filter and coffee grounds into the trash and rinse off the Aeropress. With the metal filter I first have to take off the metal filter, rinse it off and put it somewhere, and then push the coffee puck into the trash. A lot of the time I end up leaving a few drops of coffee somewhere after taking off the metal filter which I have to clean up with a paper towel, negating the paper-saving benefits of the filter many times over. The only real advantage I see to the metal filters is that it saves your ordering new filters, but at this price you can just order three packs of paper filters and go a real long time before your next order.
Works well, blocks much more coffee sediment than a french press screen, but not surprisingly less than a paper filter.

So far so good. Was a good price for two metal filters, and they seem sturdy (I had one from a different brand a few years ago that broke after a few months). The fit thing is really not an issue. Can't say that I notice a difference in taste, but I like that they're reusable.

I purchased the metal filters for my AeroPress to avoid running out of paper ones again and I liked the thought of not wasting all that paper on filters. I'm really undecided on this product right now though after using it the first time and all the water went right through, making for a no-so-great cup of coffee. After doing some reading, it's apparent that in order to use these filters, you'll need to change the way you use your AeroPress. You'll instead need to use what's referred to as the "upside down method". Google it and see what you think...it's a lot to type out.

To be honest, it sounds like a lot of hoops to jump through for a cup of coffee. However, I've done it a few times now and find that it's not terrible, and the more I do it, the less of a mess I make. I did find myself fishing the filter out of the garbage one of the first times I used it, as I'm used to just taking the end off and popping the used grounds and paper filter in the garbage.

We'll try it out for a bit and see if it's worth keeping or if we'll go back to paper filters.
